description: This reproduced portion of Delhi Rent Control Act section 14(1) states a general protection against an order or decree recovering possession from a tenant, notwithstanding contrary law or contract, subject to specified statutory grounds. Clause (b) authorizes the Controller, on a prescribed application, to order recovery where the tenant, on or after 9 June 1952, has sub-let, assigned, or otherwise parted with possession of all or part of the premises without the landlord's written consent. The supplied unit contains the opening provision, proviso, and complete clause (b), but no other eviction grounds or judicial interpretation of this language.

description: This unit records statutory provisions quoted by the Supreme Court from the Andhra Pradesh Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1960. Section 10(ii)(a), as reproduced, permits a landlord to seek eviction through the Controller where the relevant statutory conditions are satisfied, including a transfer of the tenant's lease right or subletting of the whole or part of the building without written landlord consent when the lease confers no right to do so. Section 2(ix) defines 'tenant' broadly to include specified rent-paying, surviving-family, and continuing occupants, while excluding a person placed in occupation of a building by its tenant.
evidence: transferred his right under the lease or sublet the entire building or any portion thereof, if the lease does not confer on him any right to do so
"'tenant' means any person by whom or on whose account rent is payable for a building"
limitations: This is a historical statutory quotation within a Supreme Court judgment, with preserved OCR. It concerns the Andhra Pradesh rent statute, not Delhi law, and does not provide a complete statute history or certify the applicability of the quoted provisions beyond their supplied context.

description: The Supreme Court applies the Andhra Pradesh rent statute to a company amalgamation. General Radio, the original tenant, had its property, rights, leases, and tenancy rights transferred to National Ekco under a Bombay High Court-sanctioned amalgamation and was subsequently dissolved. The Court treated this as a transfer initiated through the transferor company's petition, rejecting characterization of it as an involuntary court-imposed transfer. It emphasized the absence of the landlord's written consent and stated that the rent Act contained no exemption insulating tenancy transfers occurring through a Companies Act amalgamation. It further concluded that the transferee could not become a statutory tenant merely because the tenancy vested in it through the amalgamation order.
evidence: As such it cannot be said that this is an involuntary transfer effected by order of the court.
There is undoubtedly no written permission or consent of the respondent landlord to this transfer of tenancy right of the 1st appellant company
limitations: This is the Court's adopted application to the specific company-proposed amalgamation, Andhra Pradesh rent statute, and tenancy clause described in the source. The stored text contains OCR and page-header artifacts and does not establish a complete statute history or a universal rule for other statutory schemes.

description: This unit is the General Radio Court's report of the earlier Parasaram Harnand Rao decision concerning Delhi rent law. It recounts a tenancy whose rights were sold by an official liquidator during winding-up proceedings, with the sale confirmed by the High Court and the purchaser taking possession. According to this report, the Supreme Court in Parasaram held that section 14(b) of the Delhi Rent Control Act had sufficiently broad language to encompass not only a sublease but also an assignment or any other mode by which possession of tenanted premises is parted with. The reported holding further stated that this breadth does not exclude an involuntary sale.
evidence: the amplitude of S. 14(b) of the Delhi Rent Control Act was wide enough not only to include any sublease but even an assignment or any other mode by which possession of the tenanted premises is parted
it does not exclude even an involuntary sale
limitations: This is a reported-precedent passage within General Radio, not an independently supplied full Parasaram opinion. Its scope is the described Delhi rent-law liquidation-sale setting, and the source expressly remains an OCR-preserved historical report rather than a complete independent record of that precedent.

description: The Supreme Court found the Appellate Court's treatment of the tenancy status erroneous because correspondence and admissions established a subsisting leave-and-licence arrangement involving Esso Eastern Inc. as of 1 February 1973. The letters showed repeated renewals and supported the conclusion that Esso had acquired the status of deemed tenant or protected licensee under section 15A of the Bombay Rent Act before the later statutory acquisition. The Court therefore rejected the assumption that the licence was extinguished when Esso's rights, title, and interest were subsequently acquired under the Acquisition Act. Its reasoning depended materially on the licence having existed on the statutory date and the resulting section 15A protection already having arisen.

description: The Supreme Court describes the statutory chain by which Esso's relevant rights were transferred. Under section 3 of the Acquisition Act, Esso Eastern Inc.'s rights, title, and interest in its Indian undertakings vested in the Central Government from the appointed day; under section 5(1), the Central Government became lessee or tenant, while section 5(2) provided for renewal on the same terms if desired. A subsequent notification vested the Government's rights in Esso Standard Refining Company of India Ltd., and a Companies Act section 396 amalgamation order was followed by the company's name becoming Hindustan Petroleum Corporation Ltd. On these premises, the Court held Hindustan Petroleum protected under Bombay Rent Act section 15A.

description: The Delhi High Court gives only a prima facie view at the scheme-sanction stage. It states provisionally that a transferor company's contractual or statutory tenancy rights may pass through the court's vesting order on amalgamation without landlord consent and may fall outside section 14(1)(b). The Court expressly reserves the ultimate issue whether such a transfer nevertheless constitutes an assignment that could support eviction or other action. It explains that any landlord cause of action based on assignment arises only after amalgamation and vesting, and that the landlord retains whatever pleas the law permits. Any such eviction or civil claim must then be determined by the appropriate authority in the proper statutory or civil proceeding.
evidence: Prima facie, the rights of the transferor-company in the tenancy, contractual or statutory, are transferable on an amalgamation by virtue of the vesting order to be made by the court
Neither the amalgamation nor the vesting would deprive the landlord of any plea based on alleged assignment which may be open in law to the landlord.
limitations: The source expressly presents a prima facie, reserved view in a company-scheme sanction context. It does not finally decide whether amalgamation constitutes an assignment attracting Delhi Rent Control Act section 14(1)(b); that issue is left to the appropriate rent-control or civil proceeding. The supplied document is partial and OCR-preserved.

description: Section 44A establishes a procedure for voluntary amalgamation of banking companies. A draft scheme containing the terms of amalgamation must be separately placed before each company’s shareholders and approved by a majority in number representing two-thirds in value of those present personally or by proxy. Meeting notice must be given to every shareholder and published weekly for three consecutive weeks in at least two qualifying newspapers. Dissenting shareholders may claim the Reserve Bank-determined value of their shares if the scheme is sanctioned. After the requisite shareholder approval, the scheme must be submitted to the Reserve Bank; sanction makes it binding. Upon sanction, property and liabilities transfer to the acquiring banking company subject to the sanctioned scheme, and the Reserve Bank may order dissolution of the amalgamated company.

On the sanctioning of a scheme of amalgamation by the Reserve Bank, the properly of the amalgamated banking company shall, by virtue of the order of sanction, be transferred to and vest in, and the liabilities of the said company shall, by virtue of the said order be transferred to, and become the liabilities of, the banking company

description: Section 45 creates an RBI/Central Government regime for moratorium, reconstruction, or amalgamation of a banking company. Where the Reserve Bank considers there is good reason, it may seek a Central Government moratorium, which may stay actions and proceedings for a total period not exceeding six months and generally restrict payments, liability discharges, loans, advances, and investments. During a moratorium or at any other time, the Reserve Bank may prepare a reconstruction or amalgamation scheme when satisfied that this is necessary in the public interest, depositors’ interests, proper management, or the banking system’s interests. The scheme may regulate assets, liabilities, creditors, members, employees, proceedings, and consequential matters. After consultation on a draft, Central Government sanction brings the scheme into force and makes it binding according to its terms.

the properties and assets of the banking company shall, by virtue of and to the extent provided in the scheme, stand transferred to, and vest in, and the liabilities of the banking company shall, by virtue of and to the extent provided in the scheme, stand transferred to, and become the liabilities of the transferee bank

description: Section 9 of the Banking Companies (Acquisition and Transfer of Undertakings) Act, 1980 authorizes the Central Government, after consultation with the Reserve Bank, to make schemes carrying out the Act. Such a scheme may address the capital and board structure of a corresponding new bank and may provide for its reconstitution, amalgamation with another corresponding new bank or banking institution, or transfer of all or part of an undertaking between specified banking institutions. The Central Government may amend or vary a scheme after RBI consultation. When a scheme concerning those restructuring matters comes into operation, it binds the affected institutions, members, depositors, creditors, employees, and other persons with relevant rights or liabilities. Property, assets, and liabilities transfer and vest only by virtue of and to the extent provided in the scheme.
